one_liner.text: A 13th-century CE temple to Surya, the Sun god, built in stone as a giant chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n24 (printed page not checked)

one_liner.note: ASI and Mitra (ASI) say seven horses; UNESCO's short summary page says six.

date.text: Built in the mid-13th century CE, while King Narasimhadeva I ruled (1238–1264 CE). No exact start or finish date is known.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n16 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n41 (printed page not checked)

date.note: Dated by the builder's reign, not by a foundation inscription. ASI and UNESCO: 13th century. Behera: no exact date for start or finish. Madala Panji versions (begun 2nd or 3rd regnal year, consecrated 22nd) lack corroboration (Behera). Bahinipati et al. 2025, citing Dey 2016 and Donaldson 1985, give consecration in 1258 CE.

dynasty.text: Built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Ganga dynasty.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n16–n17 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n41 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

dynasty.note: Mitra (ASI) reports that Ganga copper-plates name Narasimhadeva as builder of a great shrine of Surya; the plates were not opened directly. Behera and Harle agree.

height.text: The surviving porch (jagamohana) is about 39 m (128 ft) high from base to top. One ASI web page gives 30 m instead. The main tower has fallen.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n44 (printed page not checked)

height.note: Mitra (ASI monograph): about 39 m from base to top. Bahinipati et al. 2025: 125 ft 8 in (about 38.3 m) above ground. ASI World Heritage web page: '30. m. square and 30. m. high'. The two ASI figures disagree. This is the surviving porch, not the fallen main tower.

deity.text: The temple is dedicated to Surya, the Sun god.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n17 (printed page not checked)

temple_type.text: The main temple, or vimana, was a rekha deula (a temple with a tall, curved tower). That tower has since fallen.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n50, n63 (printed page not checked)

intro.text: The surviving porch, the jagamohana (the hall in front of the sanctum), has a pidha roof (a roof of stacked stone layers). It looks like a stepped pyramid and rises in three tiers.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n27, n100 (printed page not checked)

intro.text: The temple had a sanctum with a tall tower and a porch (jagamohana). Both stand on one high platform carved with wheels. A separate pillared hall stands in front, in the same line. ASI calls it the nata-mandira (dance hall), but some scholars think it was a bhoga-mandapa (hall of offerings).

sources.locator: archive.org scan n2, n44, n70 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n94 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

intro.note: One detached hall, two names. ASI web page: 'nata-mandira (hall of dance)'. Behera: natamandira, adding that some scholars think it was a bhogamandapa or refectory. Mitra calls it the bhoga-mandapa but says it is 'generally believed to be a nata-mandapa (festive hall)'. Harle: the deul and jagamohana stood on a high terrace with stone wheels.

why_built.text: King Narasimhadeva I built the temple to worship Surya, the Sun god. Historian K.S. Behera says its devotional purpose is clear.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n46 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n17 (printed page not checked)

why_built.text: K.S. Behera suggests other reasons too. He thinks building probably began after the king's victory over the rulers of Bengal around 1245 CE. The king may also have wanted a temple grander than the Jagannatha temple at Puri.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n42, n48 (printed page not checked)

why_built.note: One scholar's hedged view: Behera writes 'It is likely' (start after the 1245 victory) and 'possibly' (to surpass the Jagannatha temple). No other source seen takes a position.

construction.text: Builders used three kinds of stone. Most of the temple is khondalite, which ASI's Debala Mitra calls poor-quality stone. Laterite formed the hidden core of the platform and the foundations. Chlorite was used only for door frames and a few sculptures.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n29 (printed page not checked)

construction.text: The stones were probably carried long distances on rafts along rivers. Historians think simple pulleys, wooden wheels or rollers lifted them into place.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n29 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n55 (printed page not checked)

construction.text: Iron was used too. Iron beams supported a false ceiling and the stone beams above doorways. Iron cramps and dowels held stones together.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n57, n110 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n20 (printed page not checked)

construction.text: According to a 2025 study that draws on earlier scholars, building took about 12 years and 10 months. The study dates the temple's consecration to 1258 CE. Historian K.S. Behera says the old written accounts of the building still need careful checking.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n42 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Bahinipati et al. 2025 (citing Dey 2016 and Donaldson 1985): about 12 years, 10 months and 14 days; consecrated 27 January 1258 CE. Behera 2005: the Baya chakada building accounts are 'set aside until a systematic study of the original text is undertaken'; Madala Panji versions (begun in the 2nd or 3rd regnal year) have no corroboration. No opened source gives 1246 CE as the start year.

construction.text: According to tradition, 1,200 craftsmen built the temple under the master craftsman Visu Maharana. Retellings disagree on how long they worked: 12 years or 16 years. In a popular legend, his 12-year-old son Dharmapada fixed the crowning pot (kalasa) on top.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n43–n44 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Tradition. Behera 2005 retells the legend with 'sixteen years'; Bahinipati et al. 2025 give 'twelve years'. Behera spells the name Visu or Vishu Maharana and says the name Dharmapada was first coined by Gopabandhu Das. Bahinipati et al. treat Dharmapada as a real person; that view is not adopted here.

special.text: The whole temple was designed as a huge stone chariot for the Sun god. It has 24 carved wheels (12 pairs) and seven stone horses to pull it.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n24 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Wheels: ASI, Mitra and UNESCO agree on 24 (12 pairs). Horses: ASI and Mitra say seven; UNESCO's short summary says six.

special.text: The main tower has collapsed. Only its base, parts of its walls and niches survive, beside the standing porch.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n18, n29 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

special.text: Nobody knows for sure why the main tower fell. Ideas include a sinking foundation, an earthquake or lightning, or slow decay after invaders damaged the temple. Some scholars even doubt it was ever finished.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n18 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n136, n154 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Mitra (ASI): some blame subsidence of the foundation, others earthquake or lightning, others doubt it was completed; the 'general consensus' is gradual crumbling, begun by desecration by invaders. Behera: some scholars favour earthquake or lightning, but tradition is silent about a major earthquake; some thought it was never completed.

special.text: Part of the tower still stood when James Fergusson drew it in 1837 CE. Historian K.S. Behera writes that a storm brought the last piece down in October 1848 CE. By 1868 CE only a huge heap of stones remained.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n19–n20 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n7, n153–n154 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Mitra (ASI): Fergusson in 1837 estimated the standing remnant at 42.67–45.72 m; Kittoe a year later saw one corner 'to the height of 80 ft or 100 ft'; at Rajendralala Mitra's 1868 visit it was 'an enormous mass of stones'. Behera: the last fragment fell in a gale in October 1848; the temple was deserted by 1626 but still stood to a great height then. Mitra gives no single date for the final fall.

special.text: According to a local tradition, Kalapahar, a general from Bengal, damaged the temple. He did attack Odisha in 1568 CE. But historian K.S. Behera finds no reliable evidence that he ruined Konark.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n155 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Bishan Swarup, M.M. Ganguly and Krupasindhu Mishra held that Kalapahar's removal of the top slab began the ruin (as reported by Behera). Behera: Kalapahar attacked Orissa in 1568 and desecrated the Jagannath temple, as the Madala Panji and other texts say, but these texts are silent about Konark.

special.text: UNESCO made the Sun Temple, Konarak a World Heritage Site in 1984.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n7 (printed page not checked)

special.text: In the early 1900s CE, the porch (jagamohana) was filled with sand to stop it from falling down.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n39 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n7 (printed page not checked)

special.text: Repair work began around 1901 CE. Sources give 1903 CE for the sand-filling and 1904 or 1905 CE for its completion.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n7, n162–n163 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n40 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Behera: new phase of conservation from 1901; filled with sand in 1903 by order of J.A. Baurdillon; work completed in 1904. Mitra (ASI): conservation of the porch completed in 1905. Bahinipati et al.: filled in 1903 on the directive of Sir John Woodburn; completed early in 1905.

special.text: In 1998, the World Heritage Fund gave emergency money to the Archaeological Survey of India for a structural study. In February 2000, an ICOMOS expert found no immediate danger of collapse. UNESCO then asked its staff to help India seek support for a plan to remove the sand.
special.note: UNESCO and ICOMOS records of their own acts. The Bureau 'requested the Secretariat to assist the authorities in formulating a technical co-operation request' toward a sand-removal strategy.

special.text: Early European sailors called the temple the 'Black Pagoda'. They used it, and the Jagannatha temple at Puri, as landmarks on the coast.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n14 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n7 (printed page not checked)

special.text: Art historian J.C. Harle calls Konark the last of the great Odishan temples. He adds that, as first planned, it was the largest.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

note.text: The main tower has fallen. Experts can only estimate how tall it was. Their estimates range from about 61 m to about 70 m (200–230 ft).
note.value: estimated c. 61–70 m (200–230 ft), original main tower

sources.locator: archive.org scan n44 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

note.note: Estimates only. Mitra (ASI): archaeologists conjecture 'in the range of 61 metres'. ASI web page: 'presumably over 68 m'. Harle: 'some 225 ft (70 m.)'. Bahinipati et al. 2025: 227 ft 8 in (about 69.4 m). Never use for size comparisons.

influences.text: Konark is one of many Sun temples built in India. Others were built at Modhera in Gujarat and Martand in Kashmir.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n12 (printed page not checked)

influences.text: UNESCO calls the Sun Temple 'a magnificent testament to Kalinga architecture'.

one_liner.text: The great Shiva temple of Bhubaneswar, which scholars call the most notable temple in Odisha.
one_liner.note: Panigrahi: 'by far the most notable temple not only of Bhubaneswar, but also of Orissa'. Brown: 'the finest living example of the Orissan group'.

date.text: Scholars date the main temple to the 11th century CE.
date.note: Brown: c. 1000 CE. Panigrahi: 11th century, most probably begun c. 1020–1040 CE and completed c. 1040–1065 CE. No foundation inscription is known; the dating is stylistic and indirect.

dynasty.text: The main temple was built in the time of the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings.
dynasty.note: Panigrahi treats 'Kesari' and 'Somavamshi' as the same kings. He says the side halls were later additions, possibly of the Ganga period.

deity.text: The temple is dedicated to Shiva. Hindus worship him here as Tribhuvanesvara, also known as Krittivasa and Lingaraja.

temple_type.text: According to K.C. Panigrahi, the main shrine is a pancharatha deul.

intro.text: At first the temple had only the tower shrine and its porch. The dance hall and the offering hall were added later.
Panigrahi explained that a temple's chief god came to be seen as living like a king. So the god needed an audience hall, a dance hall and a dining hall.
According to a temple chronicle, a queen had the eastern part of the temple rebuilt. Panigrahi thought she was Queen Kolavati, mother of Uddyota Kesari, and that she most likely built the porch hall.
intro.note: The chronicle (Madala Panji, as quoted by Panigrahi) names her Tulavati Rani, wife of Vasukalpa Kesari. Panigrahi calls it 'most probable' that she was Kolavati, the builder of the Brahmesvara temple, and says she was the queen of Yayati II. Both steps are his inferences.

intro.text: The main temple rises straight from the ground, with no high plinth (raised base) under it. Panigrahi contrasted this with the Parvati temple, which stands on a high plinth.

why_built.text: The temple stands in a very holy area. Percy Brown noted that the many temples in and around Bhubaneswar show how sacred this place was.
No known inscription names the builder. Historian K.C. Panigrahi thought it most likely that King Yayati II began it and his son Uddyota Kesari finished it.
why_built.note: This is one scholar's inference, not proven. Panigrahi (1961) dates Yayati II c. 1020–1040 CE and Uddyota Kesari c. 1040–1065 CE, and calls the attribution 'most probable'. He credits Yayati I with the Mukteshvara temple, not with Lingaraja. Some popular accounts name Yayati I instead; no accepted source for that has been checked.

why_built.text: Historian K.C. Panigrahi thought this temple replaced an older temple on the same spot. Some early sculptures in the courtyard may have come from that older temple.
According to tradition, King Sasanka built an earlier temple at this shrine in the 7th century CE. Panigrahi could not identify which temple that was.
why_built.note: Four Sanskrit texts credit Sasanka with a temple in this shrine. Panigrahi accepts that a stone temple stood here in the early 7th century CE. He dates the present temple to the 11th century and says the earlier temple cannot be identified.

construction.text: James Fergusson noted that the tower is built wholly of stone, from base to top. He also wrote that every stone in it has a carved pattern.
The tower is hollow inside. R.D. Banerji saw rooms stacked one above another, reached by a stair built inside the thick wall.
The temple stands in a walled courtyard about 158 m by 142 m (520 by 465 ft). The thick outer wall is made of laterite blocks.

special.text: Today Lingaraja has all four buildings of a fully developed Odisha temple: the tower shrine, the porch hall, the dance hall and the offering hall.
Many smaller shrines crowd the courtyard around the main temple. Percy Brown compared this to Buddhist shrines grouped around a great stupa.
Panigrahi wrote that the temple dominates the landscape for miles around. He called it the purest example of the Kalinga style of building.
When Ganga kings later remodelled the temple, they added some features linked to Vishnu. Panigrahi noted these are not found in other Shiva shrines.

influences.text: Panigrahi found the main shrine closely related in design to the Brahmesvara temple.

Panigrahi wrote that later Ganga kings tried to match or outdo the builders of Lingaraja. They built even grander temples at Puri and Konark. Percy Brown noted that Puri follows the same four-building plan, in one line.

one_liner.text: A small, richly carved temple in Bhubaneswar, known for the carved arched gateway in front of it.

date.text: Scholars date it to the late 10th century CE, but they differ on the exact year.
date.note: Percy Brown (1959) judged from details of its style that it was 'probably built about' 975 CE. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) argued for 966 CE. He took that year from a palm-leaf manuscript verse about a Shiva temple, and linked it to this temple through a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it. Panigrahi also places it between the Sisiresvara (c. 800 CE) and the Brahmesvara (c. 1060 CE). No inscription dates the temple. The research report's 'Brown c. 950' is not supported by Brown's text.

dynasty.text: Historian K.C. Panigrahi placed it early in the rule of the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings.
dynasty.note: This is one scholar's view. Panigrahi bases it on the temple's style and on a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it, whom he identifies as the Somavamshi ruler Yayati I. Percy Brown (1959) dates the temple but names no dynasty in the passage checked. No inscription links the temple to a dynasty.

height.text: The temple is small. Its tower rises only about 10.5 m (35 ft).
height.note: Brown: the tower is 'hardly 35 feet high'. Panigrahi: 'a height of only 34' feet, with an unclear fraction in the scan text. Rajendralala Mitra (1880) gives 'barely 3S feet' (scan text unclear: 35 or 38). None of these is an ASI measurement.

temple_type.text: According to K.C. Panigrahi, the main shrine has a pancharatha plan, and its jagamohana (porch hall) is of the pidha type.

intro.text: The temple has a tower shrine and a jagamohana (porch hall). A carved arched gateway, the torana, stands in front.

why_built.text: Rajendralala Mitra wrote that the temple stands where a mango grove once grew. Hermits had lived there, so it was called Siddharanya, 'the grove of the perfect beings'. It also had natural springs, so many temples were built there.
No known inscription names the builder. According to local tradition, a king called Yayati Kesari built it. Historian K.C. Panigrahi identified him as King Yayati I.
why_built.note: This is one scholar's inference, not proven. Panigrahi (1961) says Yayati I 'most likely' built the temple, in 966 CE, which falls in the reign he gives for Yayati I (c. 950–975 CE). He also notes that inscriptions crediting kings with building temples are absent at Bhubaneswar. Percy Brown (1959) names no builder. Panigrahi credits the Lingaraja temple to Yayati II, not Yayati I.

construction.text: The temple is small. Percy Brown gave it as about 14 m (45 ft) long and about 7.6 m (25 ft) across at its widest point.

A low, eight-sided wall surrounds the temple. K.C. Panigrahi thought it was modelled on the wall of an older temple next door, where the Siddhesvara temple now stands. He found no other eight-sided temple wall in Bhubaneswar.
James Fergusson noted that the porch has no pillars inside. Percy Brown noted that it is one of the few Odisha temples with carvings inside as well as outside.

special.text: In front stands a free-standing gateway called a torana (arched gateway). Two carved pillars hold up a round arch.
Percy Brown called the arch one of the most original ideas in the whole Odisha style. In 1961, K.C. Panigrahi noted that no other surviving temple in Bhubaneswar has such an arch.
Scholars have praised its beauty. Percy Brown called it 'a miniature gem of architecture'. James Fergusson wrote that, in its class, it was 'the gem of Orissan architecture'.
The temple is small, but its parts fit together very well. Rajendralala Mitra wrote that the eye does not notice how small it is. Percy Brown also praised its fine proportions.
Its carvings show many lively scenes. Rajendralala Mitra listed a hermit teaching a pupil, a reader with a palm-leaf book, and a lady holding a pet parrot.

According to local tradition recorded by Rajendralala Mitra in 1880, the arch was not built just for decoration. At the swing festival, a chair was hung from two iron rings on the arch. A festival image of the god was placed in it and swung.
special.note: Mitra reports what 'the people say' and does not endorse it. Percy Brown and K.C. Panigrahi describe the torana only as a gateway. Whether the custom continues today was not checked.

influences.text: Percy Brown wrote that it is believed to be the first temple of the 'Middle Period' of Odisha temple building. He dated that period to about 900–1100 CE.
K.C. Panigrahi wrote that its builder brought in a new culture, with new designs, carvings and images of gods. He said this temple divides Bhubaneswar's temples into an early group and a late group.
K.C. Panigrahi wrote that many of its features became the standard for the important temples built after it. Its porch marks the beginning of the pidha type of temple.

Panigrahi saw it as a link between old and new. Its tower shape and plan resemble older temples such as the Sisiresvara. Its porch, rounded edges and some carvings point ahead to the later Brahmesvara temple.

K.C. Panigrahi thought its arch was probably modelled on an older gateway. Parts of that older arch were dug out of a mound called Dola-mandapa, between the old temple town and the Brahmesvara temple. In 1961 they were in the Orissa State Museum.
In 1876, James Fergusson saw two 'sister styles' among Odisha's older temples. He thought about half of them follow the Mukteshvara type.

one_liner.text: A small but richly carved temple, and one of the oldest still standing in Bhubaneswar.
one_liner.note: Brown and Fergusson each call it the oldest temple of Bhubaneswar; Brown says he judges 'mainly from its appearance'. Panigrahi dates the ruined Satrughnesvara earlier, so 'one of the oldest' is used.

date.text: Scholars disagree about when it was built. K.C. Panigrahi dated it to about 650 CE. Percy Brown dated it towards the end of the 8th century CE. Older writers gave dates from about 500 CE (Fergusson) to the 9th century CE (Mitra).
date.note: No foundation inscription is known, so every date comes from style or letter shapes. Panigrahi (1961): the first or second part of the 7th century, about 650 CE. Brown (1959): towards the end of the 8th century, from its style and outside influences; he adds that the shrine may have been added after the hall. R.D. Banerji (reported by Panigrahi): not earlier than the 8th century, from the letter shapes of the planet labels on the door. Mitra (1880): 9th century, because its workmanship and stone match the Mukteshvara and Rajarani. Fergusson (1876): about 500 CE, using the traditional Kesari king list; otherwise he would have said 450 CE.

dynasty.text: Panigrahi placed it in the time of the Shailodbhava kings, who then ruled the Bhubaneswar area. But he wrote that we do not know whether any of them built temples here.
dynasty.note: This rests on Panigrahi's own date of about 650 CE, which other scholars dispute (see date). Fergusson (1876) suggested it 'may belong to the preceding dynasty', before his Kesari kings. No source names the person who paid for it.

height.text: Percy Brown gave the height of its tower as about 13 m (44 ft).
height.note: Only one height was found in the sources checked: Brown (1959), 44 ft for the tower. He gives 48 ft for the length of shrine and hall together. This is not an ASI measurement. Panigrahi gives no figure, and Fergusson gives only the plan, about 20 ft square. Mitra's description may give a size, but that part could not be read. Other figures circulate, but their sources were not checked.

deity.text: Scholars disagree about its god. Panigrahi pointed to carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Mitra reported that a sacred text, the Ekamra Purana, names its god Daityesvara. James Fergusson thought it was a Vishnu temple.
deity.note: Panigrahi (1961) notes carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Mitra (1880) reports that the Ekamra Purana calls its god Daityesvara, and he reads some porch panels as scenes from Rama's life. Fergusson (1876) judged it Vaishnava from its name and wall carvings. No source checked says outright which god is worshipped here today.

intro.text: The temple has two parts: a tower shrine (deul) and a porch hall (jagamohana) in front of it. N.K. Bose showed that the base of its wall (pabhaga) has three mouldings.

sources.locator: scan leaves 17 and 157, list of illustrations and plate caption (printed pages unverified)

construction.text: It is built of large stones laid without mortar. Percy Brown explained that the stones stay in place through their weight and balance, helped by interlocking edges.

Panigrahi wrote that this temple was built in the same way as the ruined Satrughnesvara temple. There, a hollow corbelled arch (stones stepped inwards) shows above the doorway. He explained that it kept weight off the stone beams over the door.
construction.note: Panigrahi notes that N.K. Bose thought the arch took weight off the lintel. Panigrahi disagrees about exactly which part it protects, but both see it as a weight-relieving device.

construction.text: The temple was repaired in 1903. Panigrahi noted that the repairs disturbed much of the old roof inside the shrine, though its first shape partly survives.

special.text: Its porch hall (jagamohana) is well preserved. It lets scholars study the early form of this hall. A raised central roof and stone windows with carved holes let light in.
special.note: The sources give different numbers of doors for the hall (Panigrahi two, Brown three), so no count is given.

special.text: On the shrine doorway is a carved slab of planet gods, with their names inscribed beside them. Panigrahi noted that early temples like this one leave out Ketu, the ninth planet. Later temples such as Mukteshvara include him.

Panigrahi called it the most decorated of the early temples that survive in fair condition. He noted carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Rajendralala Mitra described rows of horses and elephants carved on the porch hall.
special.note: Mitra reads the lower porch panels as scenes from Rama's life; Panigrahi speaks of scenes from Shiva's life. They may describe different panels.

special.text: Percy Brown described its tower as thick-set and heavy-shouldered, with a very wide ribbed crowning stone. He saw its shape as basic and not yet fully developed.

influences.text: Percy Brown saw links with other regions. He compared its tower and raised hall roof with Chalukya temples at Aihole in the Deccan. He linked its carved vase-and-leaf pillar tops to the Gupta style of the north.
influences.note: Brown suggests only that ideas may have been shared with the Deccan. Mitra (1880) thought the raised hall roof was borrowed instead from Buddhist monastery halls.

influences.text: Percy Brown called this temple and the Vaital Deul a stone 'primer' (a first lesson book) on how the Odisha style began. Panigrahi noted that later porch halls had only one door and were less well lit inside.
Panigrahi found at least two other damaged temples in Bhubaneswar that closely match it. One, the ruined Bharatesvara, has a similar tower and almost the same carvings on its front.

one_liner.text: The great temple of Jagannath at Puri, built by kings of the Ganga dynasty. Percy Brown called it a larger building than Bhubaneswar's Lingaraja.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaves 282–283 (printed pages not checked)

date.text: The present temple was built in the late 11th or the 12th century CE. Scholars give different years for it.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 214–215 (printed pages not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 486 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 277 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 440 (printed page not checked)

date.note: No foundation inscription was seen. Brown: about 1100 CE, with 'records' that it was not consecrated until 1118 CE. Ganguly: within Chodaganga's reign, so between 1075 and about 1145 CE. Panigrahi: 12th century, under Chodaganga. Fergusson (1876): begun soon after the Ganga kings took power in 1131. No opened source gives the often-repeated 1112 CE start.

dynasty.text: It was built by kings of the Ganga dynasty. Historians name King Anantavarman Chodaganga as the builder of the present temple.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 282 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 486 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 440 (printed page not checked)

dynasty.note: Ganguly reads the builder's name, Gangesvara (Chodaganga), from a couplet in later Ganga copper-plate grants; the plates themselves were not opened. Popular tradition names Anangabhima instead (see construction).

height.text: M.M. Ganguly surveyed the main tower before 1912. He found it about 65 m (215 ft) high, from road level to the top of its stone finial. Older books give about 58–61 m (192–200 ft).

archive.org OCR leaf 442 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 229 (printed page not checked)

height.note: Ganguly 1912, his own theodolite survey: 214.67 ft (65.4 m) from road level to the top of the stone finial; 209.42 ft from the Uttara-parsva Math compound, 5 ft 3 in above the road. Fergusson 1876 and Rajendralala Mitra 1880: 192 ft (58.5 m). Brown 1959: 'nearly 200 feet' (about 61 m). Not an ASI measurement. Figures of 226 ft and 229 ft seen elsewhere have no accepted source.

deity.text: The temple is dedicated to Jagannath. He is worshipped together with his brother Balabhadra and his sister Subhadra.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 284 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 441 (printed page not checked)

temple_type.text: According to M.M. Ganguly, the main shrine is a pancharatha deul (a tower whose walls step out in five vertical bands on each side).

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 497–498 (printed pages not checked)

temple_type.note: Ganguly: 'It is a pancharatha dewl', its corner projection showing 9 tiers. That this is the main Jagannath tower is read from context (the passage sits in his Jagannath section, between the enclosure description and the height survey of 'the vimana').

intro.text: K.C. Panigrahi explained that the temple's god was meant to live in state, like a king. So the god needed halls, such as an audience hall (jagamohana) and a dance hall (natamandira).

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 283 (printed page not checked)

why_built.text: King Anantavarman Chodaganga ruled a large kingdom, from the Godavari river to the Hooghly river. Historian K.C. Panigrahi says he built the present temple.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 282 (printed page not checked)

why_built.text: Two scholars linked the temple to a victory. James Fergusson (1876) thought the Ganga kings built it at once to celebrate winning power. Percy Brown thought a victory pillar probably stood here first.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 440 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

why_built.note: Interpretations. Fergusson: the Ganga kings replaced the Kesaris in 1131 and 'set to work at once to signalise their triumph'. Brown: 'The probability is' that the conqueror raised a commemorative column here, replaced about 1100 by the present temple. No inscription seen supports either.

why_built.text: M.M. Ganguly wrote that Puri was a holy place long before the present temple. He noted an inscription dated 1104 CE that already mentions Purushottama, a name of Puri's god.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 485, 487 (printed pages not checked)

why_built.note: Ganguly cites the Nagpur Prasasti of a Malava ruler, dated 1104 CE. The inscription's own edition was not opened.

why_built.text: Historian K.C. Panigrahi thought King Yayati I built an earlier Jagannath temple here in the 10th century CE. He wrote that nothing of it can be seen now.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 277 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 487 (printed page not checked)

why_built.note: The Yayati I attribution is Panigrahi's, partly based on the Madala Panji chronicle, which he says confuses the two Yayatis. Ganguly agrees an earlier temple stood here but names no builder. Unproven.

construction.text: According to popular tradition, King Anangabhima built the temple. Historians M.M. Ganguly and K.C. Panigrahi credit Chodaganga, with Anangabhima adding to it later.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 485, 488 (printed pages not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 47 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Ganguly: popular belief credits 'Anianka Bhim Deva, the 5th king of the Ganga dynasty', but the copper-plates place the temple earlier; Anangabhima's name probably survives because he built 'the important appurtenances'. Panigrahi: built by Chodaganga 'and his successor Anangabhima in the twelfth century'. Which Anangabhima is not settled; no opened source says it was completed under Anangabhima III.

construction.text: Percy Brown wrote that at first the temple had only the tower shrine and its porch hall. He thought the dance hall and offering hall were added in the 14th or 15th century CE.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 11, 215 (printed pages not checked)

construction.note: Ganguly (OCR leaf 488) reports that the offering hall and the inner wall are ascribed to King Purushottama Deva, of the later 15th century; that is a chronicle attribution.

construction.text: Percy Brown thought sea air probably decayed the old stonework. Later repairs covered the tower with cement. Brown felt the cement made it look heavy.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaves 497–498 (printed pages not checked)

construction.text: A photograph caption in Percy Brown's book points out iron beams in the dance hall ceiling. In 1912, M.M. Ganguly described steel beams and old rails holding up the lowest layer of the porch hall's roof.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 191 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 503 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Brown's caption does not say whether the iron beams are original or later. Ganguly's steel beams and rail columns are modern supports.

special.text: The temple has four buildings in one straight line: the tower shrine, the porch hall, the dance hall and the offering hall. Together they are about 94 m (310 ft) long.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 504 (printed page not checked)

special.text: A high outer wall of laterite stone surrounds the temple grounds. It is about 6–7 m (20–24 ft) high and about 203 m by 195 m (665 by 640 ft).

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 494 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Laterite is named by Ganguly only. The inner enclosure is 420 by 315 ft in Ganguly and Fergusson but 440 by 350 ft in Brown. Brown also speaks of three encircling walls, 'the Three Garlands'; Ganguly and Fergusson describe two.

special.text: The outer wall has a gate on each of its four sides. The eastern gate, thought of as the most important, is the Lion Gate. Two huge lion figures stand on either side of it.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 494 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

special.text: A tall stone pillar stands in front of the eastern gate. M.M. Ganguly and Percy Brown both say it was brought here from the Sun Temple at Konark.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 184, 488 (printed pages not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 218 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Ganguly calls it the Aruna-stambha and gives its total height as 34 feet (OCR leaf 494). No source seen dates the move.

special.text: Percy Brown wrote that some 30 or 40 smaller shrines stand around the main temple, inside the walls.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

special.text: The dance hall's roof rests on 16 pillars in four rows. Percy Brown called it the only true pillared hall of this kind in Odisha.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

special.text: Percy Brown noted that the temple stands on raised ground. Its tall tower is a landmark across the flat land for many kilometres around.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

influences.text: Percy Brown wrote that the temple follows the same plan as Bhubaneswar's Lingaraja temple. K.C. Panigrahi thought the Ganga kings wanted to match or outdo the builders of Lingaraja.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 283 (printed page not checked)

influences.text: Percy Brown saw progress in its design. He found the tower's outline improved, with a more graceful curve at its shoulder than at Lingaraja.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

influences.text: Percy Brown noticed that its gateways and walled courtyards resemble South Indian temple plans of the same period. He thought this was more than a coincidence.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

influences.note: Brown compares the principle (gateways and extra enclosures, like Dravidian pylons and prakarams), not the look: he says the gateways 'bear no resemblance to the gopuram type'.

influences.text: The Puri temple is older than the Sun Temple at Konark. M.M. Ganguly pointed to a carving of Jagannath found in Konark's ruins as one sign of this.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 214, 218 (printed pages not checked)

influences.note: Brown dates Puri to about 1100 CE and Konark to the 13th century. Fergusson (1876) had the order the other way round.
